newsitem.title: UK: UK's SMMT says NCAP family car tests "flawed".
newsitem.headline: UK's SMMT says NCAP family car tests "flawed".

text.p: Britain's motor car industry said on Tuesday that crash tests by the New Car Assessment Programme (NCAP) on family-sized cars were flawed and its star rating system too simplistic to aid consumer choice.

"The scope of these laboratory tests is so limited that they cannot represent the full range of real life accident situations...they tell only part of the story," the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) said in response to the latest NCAP results.
Only one family car out of 13 -- Volvo's S40 -- got the full four stars in the NCAP tests, sponsored by Britain's Department of Transport and European consumer groups.
Five cars got three stars -- Ford's Mondeo, Vauxhall's Vectra, Volkswagen's Passat, Nissan's Primera and Renault's Laguna.
The runners-up with two stars were Rover's 620, Audi's A4, BMW's 316, Citroen's Xantia, Mercedes' C180, Saab's 900 and Peugeot's 406.
The SMMT noted that all the cars easily passed the 1998 European legal crash protection standards, which amounts to a one-star rating in the NCAP system.

The NCAP test goes beyond existing requirements -- which examine only frontal impact -- by assessing front and side impacts and the effect on pedestrians. Also, it is conducted at 40 mph (64 kph), faster than the existing makers' approval test at 31 mph (50 kph).
But the SMMT warned the star rating was a "trivialisation of an important issue".
It said the NCAP tests were flawed, failing to take into account safety features such as anti-locking brakes or passenger airbags.
Also, the tests were based on one model from each range and examined only two types of impact while car makers put their products through front-end, rollover and rear-end tests, the SMMT said.

"To star cars for safety on the basis of two tests, ignoring other factors such as handling and braking characteristics, the provision of active and passive safety devices and real-life accident experience, is insufficient for accurate consumer guidance," the SMMT said.

Tuesday's results were the second round of tests in the NCAP. In February, superminis were run through the programme, eliciting praise from consumer groups for the information provided but attracting severe criticism from car companies.

The SMMT acknowledged it was important to provide consumers with safety information but said it would not expect car makers to use the results in their advertising "because they do not accept them to be a true measure of the safety of their products".
It said the NCAP and Britain's Department of Transport recognised that the tests contained anomalies and that meetings would be held this month for car makers to advise on potential revisions.
